title: Chapter LVIII

teacherSummary.text: Walking out together, Elizabeth thanks Darcy for what he did for Lydia. He says he thought only of her, and renews his proposal; she accepts. They admit how each has changed: he was proud and selfish, she prejudiced. Lady Catherine's visit, he says, gave him hope.

vocabulary.definition: The act, or the faculty, of looking back on things past
vocabulary.context: Your retrospections must be so totally void of reproach, that the contentment arising from them, is not of philosophy, but what is much better, of ignorance.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “retrospection”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Bingley and Jane, however, soon allowed the others to outstrip them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “outstrip”: out- (Old English ut, "out"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Having no example or similar case
vocabulary.context: I can no longer help thanking you for your unexampled kindness to my poor sister.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “unexampled”: un- (Old English un-, "not") + -ed (Old English -ed, past or "having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: “We will not quarrel for the greater share of blame annexed to that evening,” said Elizabeth.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “annex”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: I had narrowly observed her during the two visits which I had lately made her here; and I was convinced of her affection.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “narrowly”: -ly (Old English -lice, "in the manner of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To put to a wrong use
vocabulary.context: After abusing you so abominably to your face, I could have no scruple in abusing you to all your relations.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “abuse”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Having a due sense of benefits received
vocabulary.context: Ever since I have known it, I have been most anxious to acknowledge to you how gratefully I feel it.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “grateful”: -ful (Old English -full, "full of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: After walking several miles in a leisurely manner, and too busy to know anything about it, they found at last, on examining their watches, that it was time to be at home.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “watches”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: A proposition antecedently supposed or proved
vocabulary.context: For though your accusations were ill-founded, formed on mistaken premises, my behaviour to you at the time had merited the severest reproof.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “premise”: pre- (Latin prae, "before"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To follow out or through to the end
vocabulary.context: Now was the moment for her resolution to be executed, and, while her courage was high, she immediately said—
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “execute”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Proposals during walks were among the few private moments a courting couple had.

significance: Mutual change makes the resolution earned rather than merely romantic.
discussionQuestions: How have both characters changed, and who changed more?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with marriage and money?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter LVIII,” how does Austen show the second proposal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter LVIII develops the idea of the second proposal. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter LVIII to complicate the reader's understanding of the second proposal. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter LVIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the second proposal responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter LVIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the second proposal. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: How have both characters changed, and who changed more? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are retrospections, outstrip, unexampled, annexed, narrowly. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Your retrospections must be so totally void of reproach, that the contentment arising from them, is not of philosophy, but what is much better, of ignorance.” Webster's says: The act, or the faculty, of looking back on things past. Now the word history: “retrospection”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “outstrip”: out- (Old English ut, "out"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “unexampled”: un- (Old English un-, "not") + -ed (Old English -ed, past or "having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Proposals during walks were among the few private moments a courting couple had. Why does this chapter matter? Mutual change makes the resolution earned rather than merely romantic. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to the second proposal.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Plot.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Theme, Plot: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter LVIII,” how does Austen show the second proposal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the second proposal, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes the second proposal. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
